title: ALMA beneath the stars
caption: ALMA antennas beneath the Milky Way, Chajnantor plateau, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at ALMA, Chajnantor plateau, Chile

recognition.text: Published in the ESO image archive. No published rating.

story: An eerie green glow lights up antennas of the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, ALMA, on the Chajnantor Plateau, high in Chile's Atacama Desert. Overhead, the familiar glow of the Milky Way and the Magellanic Clouds stands out among a sea of stars.

ALMA is made up of many dish-shaped antennas. Instead of collecting visible light, like the camera that took this photograph, they gather light at millimetre and submillimetre wavelengths, which our eyes cannot see. Working together, the antennas act as a single, much larger telescope.

The sky above them holds three galaxies at once. The Milky Way is our home, seen from inside as a band of light. The Large and Small Magellanic Clouds are smaller neighbouring galaxies, visible from the Southern Hemisphere as detached, hazy patches beside it.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph taken in visible light with a camera at ALMA. The camera settings and colour processing are not published.
understand.eye: A long exposure collects much more light than the eye can, so the Milky Way and the Magellanic Clouds appear brighter than they would to a visitor.

explore: The caption does not say where the green light comes from; it simply describes it as an alien-looking glow on the antennas. Its source remains a small mystery of the picture.
alt: Dish antennas lit by a green glow on a high plateau, with the Milky Way and the Magellanic Clouds in a starry sky above.
